entities.name: St. Paul's Cathedral
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
St Paul's Cathedral in London is the masterpiece of Sir Christopher Wren, built between 1675 and 1710 CE on the site of Old St Paul's Cathedral destroyed in the Great Fire of London (1666), and the spiritual centre of the Church of England. Its iconic dome — 111 metres tall, the second-largest cathedral dome in the world after St Peter's in Rome — has dominated London's skyline for 300 years and became a symbol of British national resilience during the Second World War when the cathedral miraculously survived the Blitz.

Old St Paul's Cathedral, built from 1087, was the largest church in medieval England and one of Europe's great cathedrals. The Great Fire of London (September 1666) destroyed it entirely. Christopher Wren submitted five designs before the final was approved — the 'Warrant Design' — though Wren continued modifying it throughout construction. The dome uses an innovative triple-shell design: an inner dome visible from the interior, a brick cone supporting the stone lantern above, and an outer lead-covered dome visible from the city.

St Paul's hosted the funerals of Horatio Nelson (1806), Arthur Wellesley Duke of Wellington (1852), Winston Churchill (1965), and the weddings of Prince Charles and Diana Spencer (1981). The wartime photograph of St Paul's dome rising through smoke and flames during the December 1940 Blitz became one of Britain's most iconic images — used by the Ministry of Information to demonstrate national resilience.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: St Paul's Cathedral's survival of the 1940 Blitz while serving as the focal point of British national resilience — immortalized in photographs — made it not merely a cathedral but the symbol of a nation refusing to yield.
